\paragraph{Token specialization and routing.}
The strict division of labor between image and readout tokens suggests that the LLM does not blend modalities uniformly across token types.
Instead, visual information flows through image tokens while the readout token selectively attends to instruction tokens.
The three-condition comparison (untrained $\to$ Llama-2 base $\to$ VLA-trained: 0/32 $\to$ 9/32 $\to$ 25/32 instruction-dominant heads) reveals that routing develops incrementally: language pretraining contributes partial instruction-attending structure, and VLA fine-tuning actively reorganizes attention beyond this inherited prior.
The $9 \to 25$ head amplification during fine-tuning, combined with concentrated training effects at the readout token ($R^2$ $+0.069$) and minimal image representation changes ($\Delta \leq 1.7\%$; Appendix~\ref{sec:training_effect_summary}), suggests that VLA training primarily targets the readout token's integration function.

\paragraph{RSA--$R^2$ peak offset.}
The $R^2$ plateau (L8--L16) encompasses and partially precedes the RSA peak (L12). This suggests that maximal geometric alignment does not coincide with maximal decodability.
Training causes these peaks to converge on LIBERO-Goal (RSA L12, $R^2$ L13) but not on LIBERO-Spatial (6-layer gap), which may reflect benchmark-specific alignment.

\paragraph{Implications for VLA design.}
Three practical considerations emerge.
\emph{First}, vision encoder pretraining quality is the primary design lever; investing in stronger self-supervised encoders may yield larger gains than scaling the LLM.
\emph{Second}, since image tokens are purely visual, VLA architectures should optimize the routing from image tokens to the readout position.
Our layer-wise analysis identifies L8--L13 as the range containing the most action-relevant representations, which may inform future action head placement decisions, though validating any specific architectural change would require policy rollout experiments.
\emph{Third}, instruction invariance ($|\Delta| < 0.006$) combined with the routing mechanism suggests that instructions influence action selection \emph{solely} through the readout token rather than by modulating visual representations~\cite{grant2026}.

Token specialization and routing. The strict division of labor between image and readout tokens
suggests that the LLM does not blend modalities uniformly across token types. The three-condition
comparison (0/32 → 9/32 → 25/32 instruction-dominant heads) shows that routing develops incrementally: language pretraining seeds partial instruction-attending structure, and VLA fine-tuning
actively reorganizes attention beyond this prior, with effects concentrated at the readout token (R2
+0.069) rather than image representations (∆ ≤ 1.7%).

Implications for VLA design. Two practical considerations emerge. First, vision encoder pretraining quality is the primary design lever; stronger self-supervised encoders may yield larger gains
than scaling the LLM. Second, since image tokens are purely visual and instructions route solely
through the readout token (|∆| < 0.006; [3]), VLA architectures should optimize routing to the
readout position. Our analysis identifies L8–L13 as the most action-relevant layer range, though
validating specific architectural changes would require policy rollout experiments.

Limitations. We study a single model family (OpenVLA-7B) on LIBERO tabletop tasks; generalization to other architectures (e.g., RT-2 [1], π0 [11]), locomotion, or dexterous manipulation
remains open. MLP probes may underestimate representational capacity; RSA measures geometric
alignment but not causal contribution. Our analyses characterize frozen representations post hoc
and do not address whether architectural interventions would preserve action quality in closed-loop

\paragraph{Representation similarity and probing methodology.}
Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, originally developed in computational neuroscience, compares geometric structure between representation spaces via second-order isomorphism.
Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA)~\cite{raghu2017} and projection-weighted CCA~\cite{morcos2018} extended this approach to deep networks and enabled layer-wise comparison of learned representations across architectures and training stages.
Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)~\cite{kornblith2019} provides a related but more robust similarity index.
On the functional side, linear probes~\cite{alain2017,hewitt2019} and the broader probing methodology literature~\cite{belinkov2022} test whether specific information is linearly decodable from intermediate representations. These functional measures complement the geometric approaches by providing task-oriented evaluation.
We adopt RSA as our primary geometric metric and MLP classification probes as our functional metric, with CKA reported in the appendix.
This combination allows us to distinguish between representational structure (what geometry is preserved) and information accessibility (what can be decoded for downstream use).

\paragraph{Token-level functional specialization in transformers.}
Evidence for functional specialization among token positions has emerged across multiple architectures.
In Vision Transformers, the prepended CLS token aggregates global information for classification~\cite{dosovitskiy2021}, and Darcet et al.~\cite{darcet2024} showed that certain image patch positions are repurposed as implicit registers for internal computation.
In language models, feed-forward layers store factual associations in position-specific key-value memory patterns that differ by depth~\cite{geva2021}, and probing studies have demonstrated that different layers encode a pipeline of increasingly abstract linguistic features~\cite{tenney2019}.
These findings suggest that transformers allocate distinct computational roles to specific token positions and layers.
Our results extend this line of inquiry to VLAs, showing that image tokens remain instruction-blind across all layers while the readout token serves as the exclusive multimodal hub from Layer~1 onward.

4	VLAs fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations to produce action tokens conditioned on visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024,black2024_pi0}.
